review_notes:
I read the whole file (lines 1–64). It has one theorem, `eventually_boundary_weighted_scale`. I also read its input lemma, `eventually_boundaryPairCount_le` in BoundaryCoverageCounts.lean, which bounds `boundaryPairCount d X` by `2*C^2*X^(19/20)*log X^4`. Its only caller is `eventually_natural_boundary_small` in BoundaryCoverage.lean. The caller feeds the weight bound X^(1/100) from `eventually_boundary_weight_bound` and the lower bound X^(-1/100) on U from `eventually_boundary_inverse_main_bound` straight into this lemma.

A more general version is possible. Take any exponents a and b with a + b < 1/20, and assume M ≤ X^a and X^(-b) ≤ U. The proof would be the same, using `isLittleO_log_rpow_rpow_atTop 5` with exponent 1/20 - a - b in place of 3/100. I am not reporting this. It would only expose free exponent parameters, and the one existing use instantiates exactly the hard-coded 1/100, 1/100 to match its neighbouring lemmas. That is the kind of maximal abstraction the rubric says not to demand. Users would get little practical benefit, and the statement would become harder to read.

The `0 ≤ M` hypothesis looks removable: the count is nonnegative and the right-hand side is positive once U ≥ X^(-1/100) > 0. Deleting it belongs to the unnecessary-hypotheses experiment, though, so it is not reported here.

There is no concrete scalar type to generalise. ℝ is forced by `Real.log` and `rpow`, and X : ℕ matches the counting function `boundaryPairCount`.
